lesson.title: Named stages
lesson.text: Many process passages give each stage a technical name (coagulation, flocculation, sedimentation). The flow-chart may print the name and ask for a detail, or print the detail and ask for the name. Mark each named stage in the passage as you read; the answers are usually in the sentence that introduces or explains the name.
lesson.example: Passage: "In the final stage, called glazing, the pot is coated with liquid glass." Box: "(1) ______: pot coated with liquid glass". Answer: glazing.

questions.evidence: an intake, where screens stop large objects such as leaves, branches and fish from entering.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.evidence: Chemicals, often aluminium or iron salts, are added to the water.
questions.explanation: "Aluminium or iron" is already in the box.

questions.evidence: the particles form larger clumps known as floc.
questions.explanation: "Called" = "known as".

questions.evidence: The sludge that collects on the bottom is removed.
questions.explanation: The heavy floc sinks and becomes the sludge that is removed.

questions.evidence: The water passes through layers of sand and gravel, and sometimes charcoal.
questions.explanation: "Sand, gravel and sometimes" is already in the box.

questions.evidence: Chlorine is the most common disinfectant.
questions.explanation: "Usually" = "most common". "Ozone" and "ultraviolet light" are alternatives used by some plants.

questions.evidence: fluoride is also added to help prevent tooth decay.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

lesson.title: Word banks with similar options
lesson.text: A word bank may contain two options that are similar in meaning, such as "kiln" and "oven", or "frost" and "wind". Only one matches what the passage actually says. When two options both seem possible, go back to the passage sentence and choose the one that is supported, not the one that sounds most likely.
lesson.example: Passage: "The pots are dried in the sun." Options: A sun B fire. Answer: A, even though pots are also later fired.

questions.evidence: Clay is dug from pits, often close to the brickworks.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.evidence: during which rain and frost break it down.
questions.explanation: J (wind) is similar in type but is not mentioned.

questions.evidence: Sand may be added to reduce shrinking.
questions.explanation: Sand is also used to dust the mould, but here it matches the mixing stage.

questions.evidence: a lump of clay is thrown into a wooden mould dusted with sand.
questions.explanation: This is the hand-making method.

questions.evidence: a long continuous column ... which is then cut into individual bricks by wires.
questions.explanation: This is the extrusion method.

questions.evidence: must be dried slowly before firing, otherwise they may crack.
questions.explanation: H (melting) is not mentioned.

questions.evidence: the bricks are fired in a kiln at temperatures of around 1,000 degrees Celsius.
questions.explanation: B (oven) has a similar meaning, but the passage says kiln.

lesson.title: Follow the right branch
lesson.text: When a flow-chart divides, each branch begins with a condition, such as "star similar to the Sun" or "star over eight times the Sun's mass". The passage usually describes one branch completely and then the other, often with words such as "by contrast", "however" or "for larger stars". Before you answer a gap in a branch, find the sentence in the passage that matches the condition at the top of that branch.
lesson.example: Branch: "small dogs: live about (1) ______ years". Passage: "Large breeds live around eight years, whereas small breeds often reach fifteen." Answer: fifteen, not eight.

questions.evidence: it begins to collapse under gravity.
questions.explanation: The shock wave from an exploding star may start the process, but the collapse itself happens "under gravity", which matches the box.

questions.evidence: a hot, dense ball, known as a protostar, forms at the centre.
questions.explanation: "At the centre" is already in the box. It is not yet a "main-sequence star".

questions.evidence: At this point, nuclear fusion begins.
questions.explanation: "Nuclear" is already in the box.

questions.evidence: hydrogen nuclei join together to form helium.
questions.explanation: "Converted into" = "join together to form". Iron is produced only later, in massive stars.

questions.evidence: The small, extremely hot core that remains is known as a white dwarf.
questions.explanation: The left branch is the Sun-like star. A "planetary nebula" is formed by the outer layers, not the core.

questions.evidence: the outer layers are blasted into space in a gigantic explosion called a supernova.
questions.explanation: The right branch is the star over eight times the Sun's mass.

questions.evidence: The collapsed core becomes an incredibly dense neutron star or, if the original star was very massive, a black hole.
questions.explanation: "Neutron star" is already in the box.

lesson.title: When the passage is not in chronological order
lesson.text: In medium and hard passages, the writer may not describe the process strictly in order. A paragraph may mention a later stage before an earlier one, or add background between stages. Use the flow-chart, not the passage, to decide the order of events, and look for time words such as "before", "once", "only after" and "at the final stage" to place each detail.
lesson.example: Passage: "Before the concert, the orchestra rehearses for weeks. The players are chosen by audition." Flow-chart order: audition → rehearsal → concert.

questions.evidence: researchers write up their work in a manuscript ... and submit it to the journal of their choice.
questions.explanation: The singular noun fits "a". "Methods, results and conclusions" are parts of the manuscript.

questions.evidence: Such papers receive what is known as a desk rejection.
questions.explanation: "A large proportion" = "many papers".

questions.evidence: the manuscript is sent to two or three independent specialists.
questions.explanation: "Independent" is already in the box, so writing "independent specialists" would repeat a word.

questions.evidence: evaluate the reasoning behind the conclusions.
questions.explanation: The verb "evaluate" is in the box. "Methods" and "conclusions" are also in the box.

questions.evidence: may ask the authors to carry out additional experiments before the work can be accepted.
questions.explanation: "Request" = "ask". Paragraph C says reviewers cannot repeat experiments themselves, which is a different point.

questions.evidence: to accept the manuscript as it is ... to reject it, or to ask the authors for revisions.
questions.explanation: This is the third of the editor's options.

questions.evidence: return it with a detailed response to each point raised by the reviewers.
questions.explanation: "Detailed" is already in the box.

lesson.title: Choosing between similar numbers
lesson.text: Process passages often contain several numbers for different stages, such as the time for one step and the time for the whole process. Before writing a number, read the words around it in the passage and check that they describe the same stage as the box. Words such as "in total", "the whole process" and "this stage alone" are important signals.
lesson.example: Passage: "Drying takes ten days; the whole process lasts a month." Box: "leaves dried for (1) ______ days". Answer: 10.

questions.evidence: usually on the west bank of the Nile.
questions.explanation: "West bank" is already in the box.

questions.evidence: A long hook was pushed in through the nose.
questions.explanation: "Hook" is already in the box.

questions.evidence: stored in four containers known as canopic jars.
questions.explanation: "Jars" is already in the box, so the answer is only the adjective.

questions.evidence: The body was then covered and packed with natron, a type of salt ... which absorbed moisture.
questions.explanation: "Salt" is a more general word; the passage names the substance as natron, which is the precise answer.

questions.evidence: This drying stage lasted about 40 days.
questions.explanation: 70 days is the time for the entire process, not the drying stage.

questions.evidence: the empty body was stuffed with linen, sawdust and sometimes leaves.
questions.explanation: "Linen" is already in the box. "Leaves" were used only "sometimes"; "sawdust" is the item listed with linen.

questions.evidence: the embalmers placed small protective charms, called amulets, between the layers.
questions.explanation: A mask was placed over the face, not between the layers.

lesson.title: Word banks that test paraphrase and word form
lesson.text: At medium level, the options in a word bank are rarely the same words as the passage. "Rises" may appear as "builds", and "destroyed" as "killed". Some options are also distractors because they are the wrong word form: an adjective cannot fill a gap that needs a verb. Check the grammar of each box before you look at the list.
lesson.example: Box: "the mixture (1) ______ overnight". Options: A thickens B thick. Only A, a verb, fits.

questions.evidence: Gardeners call nitrogen-rich materials ... 'greens'.
questions.explanation: J (browns) are the carbon-rich materials, which are the other part of the mix.

questions.evidence: they produce heat, and the temperature inside a well-made heap rises quickly.
questions.explanation: "Builds" is a paraphrase of "rises", and it is a verb that fits after "heat".

questions.evidence: temperatures this high kill most weed seeds and disease-causing organisms.
questions.explanation: The passive form "are killed" fits the box. C (preserved) has the opposite meaning.

questions.evidence: the heap should be turned ... which mixes the material and lets air into the middle.
questions.explanation: The microorganisms "need oxygen", and turning lets air in. G (water) is added only "if the heap is too dry", which is not the reason for turning.

questions.evidence: the heap gradually cools down. In this cooler phase, fungi and larger creatures such as worms ... move in.
questions.explanation: The verb matches, and the time sequence is correct.

questions.evidence: they can break down tough materials such as woody stems.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.evidence: It also increases water retention.
questions.explanation: "Water" is already in the box, so G cannot be the answer.

lesson.title: Three branches, one gap each
lesson.text: Some flow-charts split into three or more branches, one for each product or outcome, and then join again. The passage usually describes the branches in a single paragraph, often in a list. Match each branch to its own sentence, and be careful with numbers and storage conditions, because the three branches will contain similar information.
lesson.example: Passage: "Apples keep for months in a cold store; strawberries last only two days." Branch: "strawberries: last (1) ______". Answer: two days.

questions.evidence: This test measures the level of haemoglobin.
questions.explanation: "Level" is already in the box.

questions.evidence: around 470 millilitres of blood ... is collected into a sterile bag.
questions.explanation: "A little under a pint" is more than two words and is only an approximation; the unit must be included with the number.

questions.evidence: screened for infections such as hepatitis and HIV.
questions.explanation: "Hepatitis and HIV" are examples; the general noun fits "screened for".

questions.evidence: it is spun at high speed in a centrifuge.
questions.explanation: "Spun" is already in the box.

questions.evidence: White cells are removed by filtering.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.evidence: Plasma ... is frozen and can be stored for up to three years.
questions.explanation: The middle branch is plasma; red cells are refrigerated.

questions.evidence: they must be stored at room temperature and constantly shaken, and they last only seven days.
questions.explanation: The right branch is platelets; 35 days is the figure for red cells.

questions.evidence: the components are matched to the patient's blood group and given by transfusion.
questions.explanation: The branches join again here.

lesson.title: Technical vocabulary
lesson.text: Craft and technology passages often introduce special terms, explained in the same sentence ("a thin strip called the purfling"). When the flow-chart gives the description, the answer is the technical term; when the flow-chart gives the term, the answer is part of the description. Read both halves of the explanation in the passage.
lesson.example: Passage: "The potter uses a wheel-head, the flat disc that spins." Box: "clay placed on the (1) ______". Answer: wheel-head.

questions.evidence: the back, sides and neck are made from maple.
questions.explanation: "Spruce" is already in the box for the top.

questions.evidence: the wood must be seasoned, which means that it is stored for years.
questions.explanation: "Stored for years" is already in the box as the explanation, so the answer is the term the passage defines.

questions.evidence: glued around a mould, a wooden form with the outline of the instrument.
questions.explanation: "Hot iron" is already in the box.

questions.evidence: The luthier repeatedly taps the plate and listens to its tone.
questions.explanation: "Test" is a paraphrase of "listens to".

questions.evidence: a long, thin strip of spruce called the bass bar is glued inside it.
questions.explanation: "Bar" is already in the box.

questions.evidence: a decorative inlay of three thin strips of wood, known as the purfling.
questions.explanation: "Inlay" is the description, so the answer is the technical term.

questions.evidence: the violin is coated with many thin layers of varnish.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

lesson.title: Cause-and-effect chains
lesson.text: Natural processes are often explained as a chain of causes and effects: A causes B, which causes C. Words such as "as a result", "this means that", "so" and "when" connect the stages. In the flow-chart, each arrow represents one of these links. If you are unsure of an answer, ask: what caused this stage, and what did it cause next?
lesson.example: Passage: "Heavy rain raised the river, so the fields flooded." Flow-chart: heavy rain → river rises → fields (1) ______ Answer: flooded.

questions.evidence: it absorbs a small amount of carbon dioxide, and it absorbs much more as it passes through the soil.
questions.explanation: "Air and soil" are already in the box.

questions.evidence: The result is a weak acid, called carbonic acid.
questions.explanation: Although "acid" is already in the box, the name of the acid is the two-word term "carbonic acid".

questions.evidence: vertical cracks, called joints, and ... horizontal divisions between the layers of rock, known as bedding planes.
questions.explanation: "Joints" is already in the box.

questions.evidence: The most rapid dissolving takes place at or just below the water table.
questions.explanation: "Most rapid" = "fastest".

questions.evidence: The passages above it drain and fill with air.
questions.explanation: The verb fits the grammar of the box, before "and fill with air".

questions.evidence: the water falling to the floor builds stalagmites upwards.
questions.explanation: Stalactites grow down from the roof and are already in the box.

questions.evidence: Where the two eventually meet, they form a single column.
questions.explanation: Both "column" and "single column" fit the limit and the grammar after "a".

lesson.title: Longer word limits
lesson.text: With NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER, you can write short phrases, but you should still write the shortest phrase that fully answers the gap. Numbers must include the unit if the unit is not in the box. Extra words from the passage do not earn marks, and exceeding the limit loses the mark even if the key word is correct.
lesson.example: Box: "water heated to (1) ______". Passage: "heated to 90 degrees Celsius". Answer: 90 degrees Celsius / 90°C.

questions.evidence: heated to about 400°C.
questions.explanation: The unit is not in the box, so it must be included.

questions.evidence: a tall steel tower called a fractionating column, which may be as tall as sixty metres.
questions.explanation: "Tall steel tower" is the description; the name of the equipment is the precise answer. "Tall" and "60 m" are already in the box.

questions.evidence: the crude oil is separated into groups called fractions, according to their boiling points.
questions.explanation: "According to their" is already in the box.

questions.evidence: The lightest fractions, collected at the top of the column, include refinery gases ... and petrol.
questions.explanation: Kerosene and diesel are collected "further down", not at the top.

questions.evidence: They include fuel oil for ships, lubricating oil and bitumen.
questions.explanation: The right branch is the heaviest fractions at the bottom.

questions.evidence: This is done using high temperatures and a catalyst.
questions.explanation: "High temperatures" is already in the box.

questions.evidence: The most important of these is sulphur, which ... produces sulphur dioxide when burned, a gas that causes acid rain.
questions.explanation: "Sulphur dioxide" is the gas produced by burning; the impurity removed from the fuel is sulphur.

lesson.title: Paraphrased boxes
lesson.text: In hard flow-charts, the boxes rarely use the passage's words. "Trigger" may stand for "set off", "carry fragments to" for "transport pieces of ... to", and "long-lived" for "persist for decades". Look for the meaning of each box, not its words. Once you find the matching sentence, the answer itself must still be copied exactly from the passage.
lesson.example: Box: "the plan was (1) ______ because of cost". Passage: "the scheme was eventually abandoned as too expensive". Answer: abandoned.

questions.evidence: anything swallowed meets the powerful acid of the stomach.
questions.explanation: "Stomach" is already in the box. Enzymes belong to tears and saliva, which are also already in the box.

questions.evidence: Damaged cells release chemicals that cause inflammation: blood vessels widen ... an infected area becomes red, swollen, warm.
questions.explanation: "Trigger" = "cause". "Innate immune response" is three words, over the limit, and is the whole second line of defence, not the effect described in the box.

questions.evidence: dendritic cells ... collect fragments of invading microbes and travel with them to the lymph nodes.
questions.explanation: "Carry" = "travel with". Phagocytes swallow microbes but do not take them to the lymph nodes.

questions.evidence: those particular cells are activated and multiply rapidly.
questions.explanation: "Activated" is already in the box; the verb that follows is the answer.

questions.evidence: B cells release antibodies, Y-shaped proteins that lock onto the invader.
questions.explanation: The left branch is the B cells.

questions.evidence: killer T cells, which identify and destroy infected cells, together with the viruses hidden inside them.
questions.explanation: "Viruses inside them" is already in the box, so the answer is the cells.

questions.evidence: A small number, however, survive as memory cells, which can persist for decades.
questions.explanation: "Long-lived" paraphrases "persist for decades".

lesson.title: Long processes with background information
lesson.text: Hard passages mix the stages of a process with statistics, history and opinion. Only some of the sentences describe the stages. Skim the passage first and mark where each stage begins; then ignore sentences that give background, such as costs and criticisms, unless a box asks for them.
lesson.example: Passage: "Critics say the test is too expensive. In the test, samples are frozen." Box: "samples (1) ______". Answer: frozen. The first sentence is background.

questions.evidence: Researchers first try to identify a target, usually a protein in the body that plays a key role in the disease.
questions.explanation: "Plays a key role in" = "involved in". "Disease" is the starting point, not what is identified.

questions.evidence: In a process known as high-throughput screening, robots test hundreds of thousands of chemical compounds.
questions.explanation: The hyphenated word counts as one word, so the answer is within the limit.

questions.evidence: The most promising compound then enters preclinical testing, in which it is studied in cells ... and in animals.
questions.explanation: "Selected" paraphrases "most promising". "Preclinical" alone does not fit after "undergoes", which needs a noun.

questions.evidence: to check that it is safe and to establish the correct dosage.
questions.explanation: "Right" = "correct". "Whether the drug works" is tested in Phase II, not Phase I.

questions.evidence: This is also the stage with the most failures.
questions.explanation: "Highest rate of" paraphrases "the most".

questions.evidence: The new drug is compared either with a placebo ... or with the best existing treatment.
questions.explanation: "Best existing treatment" is already in the box.

questions.evidence: the company submits all its data to regulatory agencies.
questions.explanation: The FDA and EMA are examples; the general term fits the box and the limit.

questions.evidence: Some side effects are so rare that they appear only when a drug has been taken by hundreds of thousands of people.
questions.explanation: "Very rare" is already in the box.

lesson.title: Word banks with near-synonyms and opposites
lesson.text: In hard word banks, several options may be possible in general, and some are the opposite of what the passage says. "Conditions" and "climates" may both seem to fit, but only one matches the passage's meaning if the passage lists more than climate. "Merged" may appear where the passage describes groups being "divided". Always confirm the option against a specific sentence.
lesson.example: Passage: "The two companies split in 2010." Options: A joined B separated. Answer: B; A is the opposite.

questions.evidence: Speciation normally requires that a single population be divided into groups.
questions.explanation: C (merged) describes the opposite, which happens when the groups are reunited.

questions.evidence: Change begins with mutations, random alterations in genetic material ... different ones appear in each separated group.
questions.explanation: "Random" is already in the box.

questions.evidence: some genetic variants may disappear, or become common, purely by luck ... This process, known as genetic drift.
questions.explanation: "By chance" = "purely by luck". I (selection) is not based on chance and is already in the next box.

questions.evidence: Each island has its own conditions: its own climate and vegetation, its own food supply, and its own competitors and predators.
questions.explanation: G (climates) is only one of the conditions listed.

questions.evidence: the beaks of finches became adapted to the foods available on each island.
questions.explanation: "Available" is already in the box.

questions.evidence: If isolation continues for long enough ... they can no longer interbreed successfully.
questions.explanation: "After long" paraphrases "continues for long enough".

questions.evidence: When humans arrived, bringing rats, cats, pigs and other predators, many such species were quickly driven to extinction.
questions.explanation: "Introduce" paraphrases "bringing".

lesson.title: Flow-charts that combine history and process
lesson.text: Some flow-charts show a sequence of events over time, from a problem to a solution and its effects, instead of a technical process. They may include dates and quantities. Look for time expressions (by 1900, in 1909, four years later) and cause-and-effect words (as a result, consequently), and check that each date or figure belongs to the right event.
lesson.example: Passage: "The idea was proposed in 1901 but not tested until 1905." Box: "first test: (1) ______". Answer: 1905.

questions.evidence: Farmers relied on ... guano ... and on Chilean nitrate, mined in the Atacama Desert.
questions.explanation: "Guano" and "Chilean" are already in the box.

questions.evidence: in 1913 the first industrial plant opened at Oppau.
questions.explanation: 1909 is the date of Haber's laboratory work, which is already in the box. 1898 is the date of Crookes's warning.

questions.evidence: hydrogen is today produced mainly from natural gas, although coal is still widely used in China.
questions.explanation: "Mainly" points to natural gas; coal is used only in some places.

questions.evidence: The two gases are compressed to about 200 times atmospheric pressure.
questions.explanation: "200" alone does not fit grammatically before "atmospheric pressure"; "times" is needed. The temperature (450°C) belongs to "heated", which has no gap.

questions.evidence: The ammonia is therefore removed by cooling, which turns it into a liquid.
questions.explanation: "Separated" paraphrases "removed".

questions.evidence: roughly half of the world's population today is fed by crops grown with nitrogen from the Haber–Bosch process.
questions.explanation: "About" is already in the box, so "half" is enough. "Four billion" is the number the world could support without the process.

questions.evidence: they use up the oxygen in the water, creating dead zones ... More than four hundred such zones have been identified in coastal waters.
questions.explanation: "Algae" is already in the box, and the effect of their decay is the answer.

lesson.title: Abstract processes
lesson.text: Economic and social processes have no physical steps; the stages are changes in behaviour, prices or expectations. The passage may use many abstract nouns (demand, confidence, expectations) that look alike. Decide which quantity each box is describing, and check the direction of change: rise or fall, more or less.
lesson.example: Passage: "Higher taxes reduce spending, which lowers prices." Box: "less (1) ______ → prices fall". Answer: spending.

questions.evidence: they set a single interest rate, known as the policy rate ... When inflation is too high, the central bank raises this rate.
questions.explanation: "Interest rate" is the general term; the box needs the specific rate set by the central bank.

questions.evidence: Central banks now publish their views on the likely future path of interest rates, a practice known as forward guidance ... the eventual rise has a stronger effect as a result.
questions.explanation: "In advance" matches "The effect begins even before the rate itself changes".

questions.evidence: raise the interest rates they charge on loans and mortgages.
questions.explanation: "Loans" is already in the box. The rates paid to savers are a different point.

questions.evidence: its value rises, and as a result imported goods become cheaper.
questions.explanation: The right branch is the currency channel.

questions.evidence: Households tend to cut back most on large purchases, such as cars, furniture and holidays.
questions.explanation: "Especially" paraphrases "most". The examples are too long and too specific for the gap.

questions.evidence: The result is lower demand for goods and services throughout the economy.
questions.explanation: "Confidence" is also mentioned in this paragraph, but it is not what becomes lower.

questions.evidence: has its full effect on inflation only after between one and two years.
questions.explanation: "One" is already in the box, so the gap needs the second figure with its unit. "Two per cent" is the inflation target, not a time.

questions.evidence: demand may fall so sharply that businesses close and unemployment rises, pushing the economy into a recession.
questions.explanation: "Unemployment rises" is already in the box.

lesson.title: Final review — putting every skill together
lesson.text: This final set combines the main challenges of Flow-chart Completion: paraphrased boxes, a branch, several numbers, technical terms, background information and a word limit of TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER. Work systematically: read the whole flow-chart, locate the start of the process in the passage, predict each answer type, check the branch conditions, confirm each number's stage, and finally reread every completed box for grammar and word limit.
lesson.example: Branch: "if no match → suspect (1) ______". Passage: "If the profiles differ, the suspect is ruled out." Answer: ruled out.

questions.evidence: Each item is sealed, labelled and recorded in what is known as the chain of custody.
questions.explanation: "Chain of" is already in the box.

questions.evidence: In the laboratory, DNA is extracted from the cells and purified.
questions.explanation: "Purified" is already in the box; the past participle fits the pattern "DNA ______ and purified".

questions.evidence: copy selected sections millions of times using a technique called the polymerase chain reaction, or PCR.
questions.explanation: "Polymerase chain reaction" is three words, which exceeds the limit, so the abbreviation must be used. This is a common trap in hard sets.

questions.evidence: today many countries analyse around twenty.
questions.explanation: "About" = "around". "Four" was used in early systems and "thirteen" in the older US system; neither describes current practice.

questions.evidence: The copied fragments are then separated according to their size by a method called capillary electrophoresis.
questions.explanation: "According to their" is already in the box, so the answer is the characteristic, not the name of the method.

questions.evidence: searched against a national database containing the profiles of convicted offenders.
questions.explanation: "National" is already in the box.

questions.evidence: scientists calculate the probability that an unrelated person chosen at random would have the same profile.
questions.explanation: The right branch is a match. "An" before the gap requires a word beginning with a vowel sound, which confirms "unrelated".

questions.evidence: DNA can move between people and objects through indirect contact, a phenomenon called secondary transfer.
questions.explanation: "Secondary" is already in the box.

lesson.title: Use the given labels to find your place
lesson.text: In an easy diagram, the passage describes the object part by part, and several labels are already given. These completed labels are anchors: find them in the passage first, and the missing parts will usually be described in the same or the next sentence. Position words, such as "at the top", "around" and "at the end of", tell you where each part belongs.
lesson.example: Given label: "handle". Passage: "The handle is fixed to a metal rod." Gap next to the handle: "metal (1) ______". Answer: rod.

questions.evidence: a handle, which is fixed to a metal rod running down the centre of the barrel.
questions.explanation: "Metal" and "running down the centre" are already in the label.

questions.evidence: The piston is surrounded by a flexible washer made of rubber or leather ... forming a seal.
questions.explanation: The label is next to the given label "piston", which helps you find the right sentence.

questions.evidence: The main body of the pump is a long tube called the barrel.
questions.explanation: "Long outer tube" describes the barrel; the answer is its name.

questions.evidence: At the bottom of the barrel is a one-way valve.
questions.explanation: "One-way" is already in the label. The "valve of the tyre" is a different part.

questions.evidence: a flexible hose carries the air to the tyre.
questions.explanation: "Nozzle" is at the end of the hose, not the part that carries the air.

questions.evidence: a gauge, a small dial mounted near the base, which shows the pressure inside the tyre.
questions.explanation: "Dial" is already in the label, so the answer is the name of the part.

lesson.title: Cross-sections with layers
lesson.text: A layered diagram shows a structure as a series of bands, from top to bottom. The passage usually describes the layers in order, either from the surface downwards or from the ground upwards. Decide which direction the passage takes, then match each layer to its paragraph. Labels may ask for the layer's name, material, thickness or purpose.
lesson.example: Passage: "Beneath the carpet lies a layer of foam, and below that, the wooden floor." Layers: carpet → (1) ______ → wooden floor. Answer: foam.

questions.evidence: Usually only about 40 millimetres thick.
questions.explanation: "mm" is already in the label, so only the number is needed.

questions.evidence: The lower of these is called the binder course, and it bonds the surface to the base.
questions.explanation: "Course" is already in the label.

questions.evidence: its job is to spread the load of traffic over a wide area.
questions.explanation: "Spreads" and "of traffic" are already in the label.

questions.evidence: the sub-base, a thick layer of crushed stone.
questions.explanation: "Crushed" is already in the label.

questions.evidence: it allows water that gets into the road to drain away.
questions.explanation: "Drain away" is two words and would exceed the limit of ONE WORD, so write "drain".

questions.evidence: the subgrade, which is the natural soil on which the road is built. ... it is levelled and compacted.
questions.explanation: The passage describes the layers from the bottom up, but the diagram shows them from the top down.

lesson.title: Labels that describe a function
lesson.text: Many labels do not ask for the name of a part but for what it does or contains, such as "where bees store (1) ______". With a word bank, find the part in the passage, read what it is used for, and choose the option that matches that use. Options that name other parts of the object are common distractors.
lesson.example: Label: "drawer: used for storing (1) ______". Passage: "The top drawer holds cutlery." Options: A plates B cutlery. Answer: B.

questions.evidence: Small gaps under the roof provide ventilation.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.evidence: The supers are the boxes where the bees store honey.
questions.explanation: A (pollen) is not mentioned in the passage.

questions.evidence: Its gaps are large enough for the worker bees to pass through, but too small for the queen.
questions.explanation: D (workers) can pass through, so they are not stopped.

questions.evidence: removable wooden frames, each holding a thin sheet of wax.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.evidence: the brood box ... is where the queen lays her eggs.
questions.explanation: The label describes the function of the brood box.

questions.evidence: In winter, beekeepers often make the entrance narrower still to keep out mice.
questions.explanation: H (mice) is what the narrower entrance keeps out, not the part itself.

lesson.title: Inside and outside
lesson.text: When a diagram shows a cross-section, some parts are at the front or outside and others are deep inside. The passage usually follows the path of something through the object: here, the path of light. Follow that path in the passage and on the diagram at the same time.
lesson.example: Passage: "Water enters through the tap, passes through a filter and leaves through the spout." Label at the middle: "(1) ______". Answer: filter.

questions.evidence: the cornea, the clear, curved surface at the front of the eye, which does most of the work of bending light rays.
questions.explanation: The label describes the part, and the answer is its name.

questions.evidence: In the centre of the iris is an opening called the pupil.
questions.explanation: "Iris" is a given label next to the gap.

questions.evidence: the lens, a transparent structure that fine-tunes the focus.
questions.explanation: The cornea also bends light, but "fine-tunes the focus" matches the lens.

questions.evidence: a ring of ciliary muscles, which change its shape.
questions.explanation: "Ciliary" is already in the label.

questions.evidence: the retina, the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.evidence: These signals are carried to the brain by the optic nerve.
questions.explanation: "Optic" is already in the label.

lesson.title: Numbers and names in the same diagram
lesson.text: Some labels need a number, such as a height, a count or a date. When the word limit allows a number, check that the number refers to the same part as the label. A passage about a building may include heights, numbers of floors and dates of construction all in one paragraph.
lesson.example: Passage: "The tower, built in 1820, has six floors and is 25 metres tall." Label: "tower: (1) ______ floors". Answer: six / 6.

questions.evidence: On top of the tower sits the cap, which can rotate, so that the sails can always face into the wind.
questions.explanation: The label gives the function; the answer is the name.

questions.evidence: The sails, usually four in number, were originally wooden frames covered with cloth.
questions.explanation: "Four" is already in the label.

questions.evidence: Most towers were between four and seven storeys high, and the tallest in England reached ten storeys.
questions.explanation: "Up to" refers to the maximum, which is ten, not the usual range of four to seven.

questions.evidence: a fantail, a small wind wheel mounted at the back of the cap.
questions.explanation: The label describes the fantail's position.

questions.evidence: The grain was raised to the top floor by a sack hoist.
questions.explanation: "Sack" is already in the label.

questions.evidence: a pair of millstones ground the grain into flour.
questions.explanation: "Pair of" is already in the label.

lesson.title: Opposites in the word bank
lesson.text: A word bank often contains an option with the opposite meaning of the correct answer, such as "washed out" and "deposited", or "added" and "removed". These traps work because both options belong to the same topic. When a label describes a process, decide carefully whether something is being gained or lost at that level.
lesson.example: Passage: "Rain removes salt from the upper layer." Label: "upper layer: salt (1) ______". Options: A added B removed. Answer: B.

questions.evidence: fallen leaves, twigs and other organic matter that has not yet fully decayed.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.evidence: its dark colour comes from humus.
questions.explanation: H (roots) are also found in topsoil, but they do not give it its dark colour.

questions.evidence: minerals and fine particles are washed out and carried to lower levels.
questions.explanation: B (deposited) describes what happens in the B horizon, the opposite process. E (sand) is what is left behind.

questions.evidence: the B horizon or subsoil, where clay and iron collect.
questions.explanation: "Iron" is already in the label.

questions.evidence: the C horizon, which consists of weathered parent material.
questions.explanation: "Weathered parent" is already in the label.

questions.evidence: At the very bottom is the R horizon, the solid bedrock.
questions.explanation: This is the lowest layer of the profile.

lesson.title: Similar technical terms
lesson.text: Passages about natural features often contain pairs of terms that are easy to confuse, such as "magma" (molten rock underground) and "lava" (molten rock at the surface), or "main vent" and "side vent". The diagram tests whether you have noticed the difference. When a passage defines a term, underline the definition and compare it closely with the position of the label.
lesson.example: Passage: "Groundwater lies below the surface; runoff flows over it." Label on the surface: "(1) ______". Answer: runoff.

questions.evidence: a vast eruption column of gas, ash and rock fragments can rise more than twenty kilometres into the sky.
questions.explanation: A "pyroclastic flow" moves down the mountain, not up into the sky.

questions.evidence: a crater, a bowl-shaped hollow at the summit.
questions.explanation: The label is the definition, so the answer is the term.

questions.evidence: alternating layers of ash and hardened lava.
questions.explanation: "Ash" is already in the label. "Lava" alone is also correct, but "hardened lava" is the full phrase and within the limit.

questions.evidence: breaking out through a side vent on the slope of the mountain.
questions.explanation: "Main vent" is already given; this label is on the slope.

questions.evidence: lava flows move slowly down the slopes.
questions.explanation: The plural fits the verb "move". Pyroclastic flows move very fast, not slowly.

questions.evidence: It travels upwards through a narrow pipe called the conduit.
questions.explanation: "Narrow pipe" is already in the label.

questions.evidence: usually between one and ten kilometres beneath the surface, lies a magma chamber.
questions.explanation: Underground molten rock is "magma", not "lava", so "lava chamber" would be wrong.

lesson.title: Several labels in one layer
lesson.text: In a layered diagram, one layer may have two or more labels: its name, what it contains, and what it does. The passage will usually describe the whole layer in one paragraph, so read that paragraph carefully and match each label to a different detail. Do not give the layer's name when the label asks for its contents.
lesson.example: Passage: "The crust, the thinnest layer, is made of granite and basalt." Labels: "(1) ______: thinnest layer" and "made of granite and (2) ______". Answers: crust, basalt.

questions.evidence: The cells at its surface are dead and filled with a hard protein called keratin.
questions.explanation: "Filled with keratin" is already in the label; the gap needs an adjective describing the cells.

questions.evidence: at the bottom of the epidermis, where there are also cells called melanocytes, which produce melanin.
questions.explanation: "Melanin" is what they produce, which is already in the label.

questions.evidence: Beneath the epidermis is the dermis ... It contains collagen ... as well as blood vessels and nerve endings.
questions.explanation: The label lists the contents, so the answer is the layer's name.

questions.evidence: hair follicles, the small tubes from which hairs grow.
questions.explanation: "Hair" is already in the label.

questions.evidence: The deepest layer is the hypodermis ... It is made up mainly of fat.
questions.explanation: "Subcutaneous" is an alternative name, but "subcutaneous layer" is two words.

questions.evidence: stores energy that the body can use when food is scarce.
questions.explanation: "Fat" is what the layer is made of; what it stores for the body is energy.

lesson.title: Adjectives and nouns
lesson.text: A label may need an adjective ("thin and ______") or a noun ("packed with ______"). Look at the words on each side of the gap. With TWO WORDS, you may need an adjective and a noun together, such as "air spaces". Make sure your answer fits the grammar of the label as well as its meaning.
lesson.example: Label: "walls are thick and (1) ______". Passage: "the walls are thick and waterproof". Answer: waterproof (an adjective, to match "thick").

questions.evidence: covered by a waxy cuticle, which reduces water loss by evaporation.
questions.explanation: "Waxy" is already in the label.

questions.evidence: a single layer of cells that is thin and transparent.
questions.explanation: The adjective matches "thin and".

questions.evidence: they are packed with chloroplasts.
questions.explanation: "Chlorophyll" is the pigment inside the chloroplasts; the cells are packed with chloroplasts.

questions.evidence: with many air spaces between them. These spaces allow gases to move easily through the leaf.
questions.explanation: The plural noun fits the verb "allow".

questions.evidence: Xylem carries water and minerals from the roots.
questions.explanation: "Water and minerals" is three words, over the limit, so write "water". "Sugar" is carried by phloem, which is already in the label.

questions.evidence: thousands of tiny pores called stomata.
questions.explanation: The label is on the lower epidermis, where the passage says most stomata are found.

questions.evidence: Each pore is surrounded by two guard cells, which open the stomata during the day ... and close them at night.
questions.explanation: "Opened and closed by" paraphrases "which open ... and close".

lesson.title: Following the flow through a structure
lesson.text: Diagrams of power stations, water systems and engines often show something flowing through them: water, air or fuel. The passage usually follows the same path from start to finish. Trace the flow with your finger on the diagram as you read, and stop at each gap to find the part the passage is describing at that point.
lesson.example: Passage: "Air enters through the filter, passes the fan and leaves through the vent." Label at the exit: "(1) ______". Answer: vent.

questions.evidence: water collects to form a reservoir, an artificial lake.
questions.explanation: The label is the definition, so the answer is the term.

questions.evidence: The intake is protected by a metal grille.
questions.explanation: "Metal" is already in the label. Copy the spelling carefully.

questions.evidence: the water rushes down a steep pipe called a penstock.
questions.explanation: "Steep pipe" is already in the label.

questions.evidence: the excess is released through a spillway, a wide channel.
questions.explanation: "During floods" matches the start of Paragraph F. This paragraph comes last in the passage, but the label is on the left of the diagram, next to the dam.

questions.evidence: Inside the generator, large magnets rotate within coils of copper wire.
questions.explanation: The turbine is given as a separate label; it is the generator that contains the magnets.

questions.evidence: a transformer, which increases its voltage.
questions.explanation: "Increases" is already in the label.

questions.evidence: the water flows out through a channel known as the tailrace and returns to the river below the dam.
questions.explanation: The spillway also returns water to the river, but only excess flood water; the tailrace is where water leaves after passing through the turbine.

lesson.title: Word banks for processes inside a machine
lesson.text: When a diagram shows a machine at work, many labels describe changes: something rises or drops, is absorbed or released, becomes a liquid or a gas. The word bank will contain both directions. For each label, find the part in the passage and ask: what changes here, and in which direction?
lesson.example: Passage: "In the boiler, water turns to steam." Label: "boiler: water becomes (1) ______". Options: A ice B steam C liquid. Answer: B.

questions.evidence: the refrigerant ... evaporates and absorbs heat from the food and air inside the cabinet.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match. The heat is released later, at the condenser.

questions.evidence: The refrigerant, now a gas, flows to the compressor.
questions.explanation: At the evaporator, the refrigerant evaporates, so it becomes a gas. C (liquid) describes the refrigerant after the condenser.

questions.evidence: A thermostat measures the temperature ... and switches the compressor on ... and off.
questions.explanation: I (fan) is not mentioned in the passage.

questions.evidence: The compressor squeezes the gas, greatly raising its pressure.
questions.explanation: J (volume) is not mentioned; squeezing a gas actually reduces its volume.

questions.evidence: the heat it took from the food is released into the kitchen.
questions.explanation: B (absorbs) is the opposite process, which happens at the evaporator.

questions.evidence: its pressure drops suddenly.
questions.explanation: H (rises) is the opposite, which happens at the compressor.

lesson.title: Words from other languages and unusual spellings
lesson.text: Passages about history often use specialist words, some of them borrowed from other languages, such as "portcullis" or "bailey". These are easy to misspell under time pressure. When you find an answer of this kind, copy it one letter at a time. A misspelled answer is marked wrong, even if you have found the correct part.
lesson.example: Passage: "The knights wore a hauberk, a shirt of chain mail." Label: "(1) ______: shirt of chain mail". Answer: hauberk, not "hawberk".

questions.evidence: the moat, a wide, deep ditch that surrounded the castle and was usually filled with water.
questions.explanation: "Ditch" is in the label; the answer is the name.

questions.evidence: a drawbridge, a wooden bridge that could be raised by chains.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.evidence: a portcullis, a heavy iron grille that could be dropped quickly.
questions.explanation: "Iron grille" is the description. Murder holes are in the roof of the passage, not a grille.

questions.evidence: Narrow arrow slits in the walls allowed archers to fire out.
questions.explanation: "Narrow arrow" is already in the label.

questions.evidence: Along the top of the walls ran the battlements, a walkway protected by a low wall.
questions.explanation: This is the name of the walkway.

questions.evidence: an open courtyard called the bailey, which contained stables, workshops, a kitchen and a well.
questions.explanation: The label is the definition.

questions.evidence: the keep, a massive tower ... served as the last refuge if the outer defences fell.
questions.explanation: "Towers" also strengthened the curtain wall, but the keep is the massive tower and last refuge.
